data.title: stacker deploy --target server writes every project to the same remote path, causing real cross-project deployment damage
data.excerpt:
produced via `stacker-projects/duplicati` colliding with a pre-existing `stacker-projects/rallly` deployment, both targeting the same `EXISTING_SERVER_HOST`, in trydirect/stacker-project-examples
- Related: #235 (same bug class, `--target local` variant)
---
Updating with a more severe detail found on further investigation: this wasn't just compose-file thrashing — **rallly's actual database volume was recreated empty**, i.e. real data loss.

\`docker volume inspect project_rallly_db\` shows \`CreatedAt: 2026-08-20T17:40:21Z\` — today, during this exact testing window — and \`du -sh\` on it shows only 8.0K (empty, no real data). Postgres now refuses to start: \`Database is uninitialized and superuser password is not specified\` (rallly's own compose has \`POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ''\`, which was presumably fine against the *original* initialized volume but fails cold-start validation against a fresh empty one).

So the actual sequence was worse than "wrote a different compose file over the old one": something in the \`--target server\` deploy path for \`duplicati\` appears to have torn down and recreated volumes under the shared \`project\` compose project scope too — not just the compose file/containers. This raises the severity from "silent overwrite" to "silent data loss" for whatever was in the previous occupant's volumes.
---
Fixed. Each project now gets its own directory /home/

data.title: macOS Docker Desktop shared mount path issue when running Kathara inside a container
data.excerpt:
reproducible issue related to shared folder mounting when Kathara itself is executed inside a Docker container.

Environment:

* macOS
* Docker Desktop
* Kathara 3.8.3
* Ubuntu 22.04 container used to execute Kathara

Problem:
When Kathara is executed inside a Docker container, shared folder mounts are generated using the container filesystem path instead of the corresponding host filesystem path.

Example generated path:

/labs/progetti/lab1/shared

instead of the actual host path:

/Users/username/dockers/kathara/progetti/lab1/shared

(where “dockers” is only an example host-side folder used to collect Docker-related projects)

Docker Desktop rejects the mount with the following error:

“Mounts denied:
The path /labs/progetti/lab1/shared is not shared from the host and is not known to Docker.”

Analysis:
The issue appears in DockerMachine.py where:

machine.lab.shared_path

is directly passed to Docker volume creation.

Since Kathara is running inside a container, this path represents the container-side filesystem path instead of the real host filesystem path required by Docker Desktop on macOS.

Proposed fix:
Introduce host/container path translation support using environment variables:

* KATHARA_CONTAINER_LAB_ROOT
* KATHARA_HOST_LAB_ROOT

Before creating Docker volume mounts, translate:

container path -> host path

Example:

/labs/progetti/lab1/shared
→
/Users/username/d

data.excerpt:
<!-- gitissue:normalized v1 -->

## Type
Bug

## Description
Under QEMU, the ubuntu-22.04 arm64 leg of `.github/workflows/release-packages.yml` sometimes fails with `qemu: uncaught target signal 11` from `ldconfig`. The failure is at `tools/ci/build-package.sh:151`. It happened with setup-qemu-action v4.3.0 and v4.4.0, and every run used the same binfmt image digest (`tonistiigi/binfmt@sha256:400a4873…`, qemu v10.2.3). It surfaced on PR #420 and passed on a rerun. Earlier runs 35811132281 and 35802233452 show the same segfault in the apt libc-bin trigger, which does not fail the job.

- [ ] Pin the binfmt image by digest in the setup-qemu step, and/or make the emulated `ldconfig` step in build-package.sh retry or tolerate a crash without masking real failures
- [ ] ubuntu-22.04 arm64 package job passes reliably

**What failed:** Candidate image run on main for prepare commit fafe9658 (v1.6.0) was cancelled by the 40-min job timeout; no image for `sha-fafe965` reached GHCR.
**Run:** https://github.com/tjakobsson/brain/actions/runs/33716434026

**Likely cause:** intermittent QEMU user-mode crash emulating arm64 node/npm; same chainguard/node (d6ca8dfc) and binfmt (400a4873) digests as the last green run, so not a version change. The arm64 layer was a cache miss because the version bump changed package-lock.json. BuildKit hung instead of failing the step after the crash.

data.title: Elasticsearch
data.excerpt:
### Name of the Script
Elasticsearch

### Script Type
CT (LXC Container)

### Does this script support arm64?
arm64 supported

### 📋 Script Details
Single-node Elasticsearch from the official Elastic repository. Requested in [discussion #5074](https://github.com/community-scripts/ProxmoxVE/discussions/5074).

**The open question from the earlier assessment — `vm.max_map_count` in an unprivileged LXC — is resolved.** Per Elastic's docs, bootstrap checks are only warnings in *development mode* (loopback binding) but hard failures in *production mode* (non-loopback), and an LXC is only useful bound to the LAN. However `vm.max_map_count` is **not namespaced**: the container inherits it from the Proxmox host. So it cannot and need not be set inside the container.

The script therefore checks the inherited value and aborts with an actionable message if it is too low:

```
vm.max_map_count is <n>, Elasticsearch needs at least 262144
Set it on the PROXMOX HOST, not in this container:
  echo 'vm.max_map_count=1048576' >/etc/sysctl.d/99-elasticsearch.conf

data.title: REST test stack: pick free ports instead of failing on 55432/8080/8443
data.excerpt:
Seen 2026-09-10 while shipping milestone 21: `bin/test-rest-stack.sh` could not run because another project's Postgres container already listened on `127.0.0.1:55432`.

Two problems, one fix:

1. The script accepts `YELUKEREST_TEST_DB_PORT` (and HTTP/HTTPS) overrides for the docker port mapping, but `YELUKEREST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` / `YELUKEREST_TEST_MIGRATOR_DATABASE_URL` in `.env` carry a fixed port. Overriding the port therefore brings the container up on one port while zapadka and the tests connect to another ("cannot connect to the target: Connection refused").
2. There is no detection at all: the failure is docker's "Bind for 127.0.0.1:55432 failed: port is already allocated", after the script has already torn down the dev stack.

Proposal, keep it simple:

- [ ] Before starting anything, probe the three ports (`nc -z` or `lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN`). If one is taken and no override is set, pick the next free port in a small range (e.g. 55432–55441) and say so on stderr.
- [ ] Derive the database URLs the script uses from the chosen port: take the URLs from `.env`, rewrite only the port (`sed` on `:<port>/`), and export them for zapadka and the test runner. The `.env` values stay the documented defaults.
- [ ] Do the probe **before** `docker compose down` so a port clash never leaves the dev stack down.

data.title: Port allocation race: concurrent sandbox creation fails with "port is already allocated"
data.excerpt:
## Summary

With `runtime.type = "docker"` and `docker.network_mode = "bridge"`, concurrent sandbox creation
fails intermittently because the server hands out a host port that another in-flight creation is
already using. The failure surfaces to the caller as HTTP 500:

```
Failed to create or start container: 500 Server Error for
http+docker://localhost/v1.55/containers/<id>/start: Internal Server Error
("failed to set up container networking: driver failed programming external connectivity
 on endpoint sandbox-<uuid>: Bind for 0.0.0.0:41106 failed: port is already allocated")
```

The port appears to be **chosen at random from `docker.port_range_*` and then handed to Docker to
bind, with nothing reserving it in between**. Two creations racing between the pick and the bind get
the same port.

## Evidence: the failure rate follows the birthday paradox

Each sandbox consumes 2 host ports, so N concurrent creations draw 2N ports from the range. If the
draws are independent and unreserved, the expected number of collisions is `(2N)² / (2 · R)` for a
range of R ports. Measured on a single node, server `v0.2.3`, `secure_runtime.type = "gvisor"`:

| Concurrent creations | Draws | Range | Expected collisions | **Observed failures** |
|---|---|-

ra trying to access `/var/run/docker.sock`, which is not the Podman rootless socket.

Steps to reproduce on Fedora Linux with rootless Podman:

Kestra fails to access the container runtime and reports an error similar to:

Since the documentation explicitly states that the provided Compose file works with Podman Compose and describes the setup as a rootless Podman deployment, the compose configuration should either: use the appropriate Podman rootless socket or explicitly document that the provided compose file requires additional configuration to connect Kestra to the Podman socket.

The Podman Compose guide could provide a Podman-specific compose override or configuration showing how to mount the rootless Podman socket, for example:

```

data.title: Root-stage mkdirs under $HOME break the user-stage volume mkdirs
data.excerpt:
A template that creates a directory under `$HOME` in its `root.Dockerfile` leaves it owned by `root`. The generated user stage later runs `mkdir -p` for every declared volume path as `${USER}`, so any volume nested under that directory fails the build.

The `jupyter` template hits this: its `root.Dockerfile` runs `mkdir -p $HOME/.local`, so a volume at `.local/share/<name>` cannot be created.

Reproduce with:

```json
[
  {
    "name": "jupyter_repro",
    "templates": ["jupyter"],
    "volumes": { "state": ".local/share/example" }
  }
]
```

`docker compose build jupyter_repro` fails with:

```
mkdir: cannot create directory '/home/user/.local/share': Permission denied
```

The generated Dockerfile shows the cause — `USER root` creates `$HOME/.local`, then the volume mkdirs run after `USER ${USER}`:

```
USER root
# --- jupyter ---
RUN mkdir -p $HOME/.local && \
    mkdir -p $HOME/.jupyter

USER ${USER}
RUN mkdir -p \
    $HOME/.local/share/example
```

Possible fixes: `chown` root-stage `$HOME` directories back to the container user, emit the volume mkdirs before the root fragments, or drop the redundant `mkdir` calls from `jupyter/root.Dockerfile` since the volume mkdirs already cover them.

data.title: docker/Dockerfile.heavy: image cannot boot with a Docker-managed volume — .omnipus is created root-owned
data.excerpt:
ed.

Verified against `release/v0.1.1` @ `aa97bcea574ebf5c3a56058b7d2095716a6f5da4`.

## Reproduce

```sh
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.heavy -t omnipus-heavy:repro .
docker run --rm -v repro-vol:/home/omnipus/.omnipus -p 127.0.0.1:5199:5000 \
  -e OMNIPUS_GATEWAY_HOST=0.0.0.0 -e OMNIPUS_SANDBOX_MODE=permissive \
  omnipus-heavy:repro
```

Observed — container exits, `/health` never becomes available:

```
Warning: could not ensure cli token: update config.json: read config.json: open /home/omnipus/.omnipus/config.json: no such file or directory
Open the dashboard / log in as admin:
  This machine:   http://localhost:5000
Error: creating log directory: mkdir /home/omnipus/.omnipus/logs: permission denied
```

## Cause

`useradd -m -d /home/omnipus` (`docker/Dockerfile.heavy:179`) creates the home directory, but **nothing ever creates `/home/omnipus/.omnipus`**. `VOLUME /home/omnipus/.omnipus` (`:184`) then declares a mount point that does not exist in the image.

Docker seeds a fresh volume from whatever is at that path in the image. Finding nothing, it creates the directory as `root:root`. The container runs as `USER omnipus` (`:182`, uid 1000), which cannot write into it.

Confirmed directly — on the unmodified image the mount point is root-owned; after creating and chowning it before `VOLUME`, the same volume comes up owned by uid 1000 and the instance boots:
